translation: Perhaps due to their frequent meetings in their local area, Miho and Satsuki have strikingly similar expressions and way of talking.
Their way of eating sweets, especially, is identical.
Using their hands adorned with nail art, they break off small pieces of the biscuits before bringing them to their mouths.
I wonder if this has always been the case—but my memory is hazy.
The minor habits and gestures they displayed during our last meeting may have faded away for all I know.
Miho is now married, has bought a used detached house in her hometown, and often has friends gather there.

Although she sometimes feels reluctant because she also works part-time tomorrow, this is the only connection with the world outside of her convenience store job and a valuable opportunity to interact with other "normal thirty-something women" of the same age, so she tries to accept Miho's invitations as much as possible.
Today as well, Miho and I were having tea at her house bringing cake along with Yukari who is also married but yet to have kids and still brought along her small child—the usual members.
At that moment, I felt for the first time that I had become a part of the world.
It was as if I had just been born.
On that day, my new self was most definitely birthed as a functioning component of the world.
For the two weeks leading up to the opening, we practiced non-stop either in pairs or with employees, with hypothetical customers.

Bowing and smiling while looking into the "customer's" eyes, placing sanitary products in a paper bag, separating hot items from cold items when bagging them, disinfecting our hands with alcohol if asked for fast food.

To get accustomed to handling money real cash was placed in our registers but our receipts were clearly marked "training", and since we were all just part-timers wearing the same uniform it somehow felt like we were playing make-believe shopping.
My sister, two years younger than me, was a "normal" child unlike me.
Yet she did not shun me; on the contrary, she adored me.
When she was being lectured by my mother for doing ordinary things that upset her, I would approach and ask my mother why she was angry.
My sister would always say 'thank you' to me after these incidents whether it was because my question had ended the lecture or because she felt shielded by it.
I wasn't particularly interested in sweets or toys and often gave mine to her.
As a result of all these acts on my part, my sister would constantly follow me around.
"Dad loved yakitori, so let's grill this and eat it today.
When I repeated my words more clearly, wondering if she hadn't heard correctly, my mother gawked in astonishment.
The lady next to her had the same reaction their eyes, nostrils and mouths opened wide at once; their faces looked so ridiculous that I almost laughed.
But then I noticed the woman staring intently at my hand, and it occurred to me that one bird wouldn't be enough.
"Should I catch some more?"
As I glanced at two or three sparrows walking closely together nearby, my mother finally snapped back to reality and cried out desperately in reprimanding tone: "Keiko!"
"Instead of eating these little birds," she explained with a strained smile,"we should bury them properly Look—everyone is crying because they're sad their friend passed away.
It's pitiful right?"  "Why? Isn't this perfect because they're already dead?"
My puzzled question seemed to leave my mother speechless.
I quickly put canned coffee, cigarettes, and an American hot dog into a small size bag.
Meanwhile, the man who had been jingling coins in his pocket appeared to suddenly remember something and reached into his breast pocket.
From this movement, I instantaneously judged that he intended to pay with electronic money.
"Welcome, good morning!"
She takes the canned coffee handed by the male customer with a slight nod.
"Ah, and one of number five cigarettes.
"Understood.
Quickly she pulls out a Marlboro Light Menthol and scans it at the register.
"Please touch for age verification.
While he touches the screen, she notices his gaze swiftly move to the fast food lined showcase; then she stops her finger movements.
She could ask 'Will you take anything else? but when a client seems uncertain about whether to buy something or not, she chooses to step back and wait.
Reacting to the faint sound of small change jingling, I turn my gaze towards the cash register.
People who deal with coins in their hands or pockets are often those who buy a pack of cigarettes or a newspaper and quickly go home, so I'm sensitive to the sound of money.
As expected, there was a man approaching the register with one hand clutching a can of coffee and the other buried in his pocket.
Quickly navigating through the store into the cash counter, ready to serve without making customers wait.
A convenience store is filled with sounds.
There is the chime when a customer enters, the voice of an idol promoting new products over the in-store radio broadcasts.
The calling of employees blends with the beep of barcode scanners.
Sounds of things being put into baskets, bread bags being held, and heels walking around the store all mix together into "the sound of a convenience store," which constantly reaches my eardrums.
